facts.text: Global temperatures dropped abruptly around 8,200 years ago, and the cool spell lasted two to four centuries.
In Greenland the temperature fell 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years; the coldest phase lasted about 60 years.
A meltwater pulse, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway draining into the North Atlantic, may have weakened Atlantic overturning by 55–62%.
Cave records from Eurasia to South America and southern Africa show it; methane fell 15%, and North and East Africa turned drier.
Its signal in the NGRIP1 Greenland ice core is the GSSP for the base of the Northgrippian, set at 8,236 years before 2000.

title: Final drainage of lakes Agassiz and Ojibway

facts.text: As the last Hudson Bay ice melted, Lake Agassiz drained almost completely in its final major drainage shift.
Neighbouring Lake Ojibway, comparable in size, likely drained at the same time, perhaps in two floods through a broken ice dam and beneath the ice.
The final drainage raised global sea level by an estimated 0.8 to 2.8 m.
The freshwater flood is the leading suspected trigger of the 8.2-kiloyear cooling.
Lake Agassiz refilled as the ice withdrew north of today's Canada–US border around 10,000 years ago, and abandoned its southern outlet by about 9400 BP.

title: Storegga Slides and North Atlantic tsunami

facts.text: Three submarine landslides at the edge of Norway's continental shelf moved about 3,500 km³ of debris along 290 km of shelf, among the largest known.
The slides set off large tsunamis in the North Atlantic; waves up to 20 m high hit Scotland and the Faroe Islands.
Tsunami sediment in Scotland lies up to 29 km inland and 4 m above today's normal tide level.
An earthquake that destabilised methane clathrate is thought to have triggered the collapse.
The tsunami may have flooded Doggerland's last low-lying land, though its impact there is debated.

title: Early farming lifts greenhouse gases (Ruddiman hypothesis)

facts.text: William Ruddiman argues that forest clearing by early farmers began raising greenhouse gases about 8,000 years ago.
CO2 rose markedly from about 8,000 years ago, and methane some 3,000 years later.
Critics counter with data from an earlier interglacial, and say all interglacials differ.

contested_note: Ruddiman's early-Anthropocene hypothesis is challenged by other researchers.

verification.title: Is the Anthropocene really worthy of a formal geologic definition?
verification.note: The 11.7 ka date is the earliest proposed Anthropocene start, at the Holocene onset, not Ruddiman's 8,000-year claim.

facts.text: The warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP.
After the 8.2 ka cold snap the climate warmed to the highest temperatures of the Holocene, and polar ice caps shrank to their Holocene minimum.
The warmest 200 years, around 6,500 years ago, were about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century.
Rain belts shifted: Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo valley got up to twice today's rainfall, and a stable climate fostered farming in China.
The warmth was followed by a slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium until about two centuries ago.

facts.text: The steppe bison, a mammoth-steppe grazer, survived in north-central eastern Siberia until about 8,000 years ago.
Bison DNA in northeastern Siberian permafrost may extend its survival to 5050–3800 BCE; the youngest North American remains, from Yukon, date to 3628–3377 BCE.

title: Rising seas split Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania

facts.text: Post-glacial sea-level rise flooded the Bassian Plain, forming Bass Strait and making Tasmania an island.
Aboriginal Tasmanians, who had walked across the land bridge about 40,000 years ago, were cut off from the mainland.
New Guinea separated from mainland Australia about 8,000 years ago, ending the single Sahul landmass.
The New Guinea land bridge was fully flooded about 8,000 years ago; over the next 2,000 years thousands of Torres Strait and coastal islands formed.

conflicts.note: Sahul page dates Tasmania's separation later

title: Final collapse of the Laurentide Ice Sheet

facts.text: About 8,000 years ago the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split into two lobes, over Quebec–Labrador and Keewatin.
Central Asia stayed at near-glacial temperatures until the ice sheet collapsed around 8,000 BP.
Its final melting, between 8 and 7 ka, was followed by a much slower rate of global sea-level rise.
Ice discharge from the collapsing sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic until 6,700 BP; ice finally left Nunavik about 6,500 years ago.

conflicts.note: Holocene glacial retreat page: North American deglaciation ran to 7,000 years ago

title: Modern Mississippi and Rhine deltas begin forming

facts.text: As sea-level rise slowed, the modern Mississippi River delta plain began to build around 8,000–7,500 years ago.
In the Netherlands, the Holocene Rhine–Meuse delta began forming about 8,000 years ago, shaped by sea-level rise and tectonic subsidence.
By switching course every 1,000–1,500 years, the Mississippi built six delta complexes; such deltas became major farming and population centres.
The Irish elk, or giant deer, survived in western Russia until around 7,700 years ago as Ice Age megafauna losses continued.
Its latest dated remains include finds at Kamyshlov and Maloarkhangelsk, Russia, from the 6th millennium BCE; it likely died out soon after.
By the early Holocene its range had shrunk dramatically; its youngest eastern records, near Lake Baikal, date to 10,700–10,400 BP.

title: Mount Mazama eruption forms Crater Lake

facts.text: Oregon's Mount Mazama, active again after 20,000 quiet years, ended in a VEI 7 eruption whose collapse left the caldera now holding Crater Lake.
A 48 km ash column reached the stratosphere; ash fell across eight western US states and three Canadian provinces.
The USGS has called it the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past million years.
Its orange Mazama Ash covers at least 900,000 km² of the northern Great Plains and reaches Greenland's ice sheet, making it a standard dating marker.
Aerosols may have cooled mid- to high northern latitudes by 0.6–0.7 °C for one to three years; ashfall drove people out, leaving one Alberta site empty for about 200 years.

facts.text: Fast sea-level rise, the 8.2 ka cooling and loss of coastal land may have helped push the Neolithic Revolution into Europe.
In Central Europe human impact first shows in pollen records from 7,500 BP, and becomes substantial after 6,300 BP.
An Early Neolithic lakeshore village at La Marmotta, Italy, dates to about 5700 BC.
From about 7,500 years ago European Neolithic farmers also crossed from Iberia into Northwest Africa.
Farming took about 2,500 years, 8500–6000 BP, to spread from the Aegean, where it appears by c. 6500 BCE, to Britain; the Baltic followed around 5500 BP.
The Gulf of Thailand, dry and arid land before 7,500 BP, was drowned by a marine transgression from 7,500 to 6,200 BP amid global warming.
Sundaland, the exposed Sunda Shelf of Southeast Asia, was flooded as rising seas followed the 8.2 ka cool period.
Its partial submergence, under way since 18,000 years ago, continued until about 5000 BC.

title: Giant ground sloth Megatherium dies out

facts.text: Megatherium americanum, a ground sloth of up to 4 tonnes and 6 m long, died out in Argentina around 5370 BC.
Its latest remains, at Campo Laborde, show signs of human hunting and butchery.
Habitat modelling suggests its suitable range had shrunk and broken up by the mid-Holocene.

facts.text: Japan's submarine Kikai Caldera produced the Akahoya eruption, a VEI 7 event and one of only six confirmed eruptions of its size in the Holocene.
Pyroclastic flows crossed the sea to southern Kyushu, up to 100 km away, and ash fell as far as Hokkaido.
A 2024 study put the ejecta at 332–457 km³, the largest eruption of the past 11,700 years.
Two large earthquakes shook the region during the eruption, and a megatsunami left deposits along western Japan's coast up to 300 km away.
It transformed southern Kyushu's vegetation and hit the early Jōmon culture there hard; recovery took nearly 1,000 years, though local pottery traditions survived.

facts.text: About 6,000 years ago the post-glacial warming trend ended and a long cooling trend began.
Neoglaciation followed the Holocene Climatic Optimum, with glaciers advancing or re-forming, though it has no single clear start.
In East Asia its start coincided with a major weakening of the summer monsoon.
In western North America, mountain glaciers that had melted away entirely re-formed shortly before 5000 BP.
Orbital models suggest this cooling trend would continue for another 23,000 years.

verification.title: Modeling the Climatic Response to Orbital Variations

facts.text: Global sea level, rising steadily since 20,000 years ago, levelled off about 6,000 years ago and has been fairly stable since.
In places sea level overshot today's: off Santa Catarina, Brazil, it peaked about 2.1 m above present 5,800–5,000 BP.
Rising water drowned the last land bridges, such as the southern Kuril link to Hokkaido around 6,000 BP.
The rate of rise fell from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm, ushering in some 4,000 years of near-stable sea level.

title: End of the African humid period; Sahara dries

facts.text: The African humid period ended about 6,000–5,000 years ago, often put at 5,500 BP, and the green Sahara began turning into desert.
North of the monsoon belt drying came in one step within 500 years; dust off Mauritania rose sharply within a few centuries.
Orbital shifts cut rainfall and raised temperatures; overgrazing has also been proposed as a trigger.
Lakes dried, vegetation vanished, and dust from basins like Bodélé, now Earth's largest dust source, grew; shrinking wetlands lowered atmospheric methane.
North Africa's population fell within a millennium, and many inner-Arabian settlements were abandoned about 5,300 years ago.

facts.text: Around 3900 BCE an aridification event struck the Sahara.
Pastoral herders, facing a drier climate, were forced to migrate into the Nile valley to survive.
In Hoti Cave, Arabia, the Indian monsoon retreated southward about 5,900 years ago.
The Sahara's desiccation may have driven the spread of farming in the Sahel.
It corresponds to Bond event 4, about 3900 BC, one of eight North Atlantic ice-rafting events; the Sahara had re-formed by 3500–3000 BC.

title: Last mammoths of St. Paul Island, Alaska

facts.text: A small woolly mammoth population survived on St. Paul Island, Alaska, until about 3750 BC, long after mainland mammoths vanished.
There is no evidence of prehistoric people on the island.
Bone dates and environmental proxies tightly constrain their end to around 5,600 years ago, most likely as fresh water ran short.

facts.text: The Piora Oscillations, two cold periods in Alpine climate history named after Switzerland's Val Piora, coincided with the end of the African humid period.
From 5,600 to 5,000 years ago cooling and erratic rainfall were widespread; the Arctic cooled, sea ice spread and Atlantic overturning weakened.
Around 5,375 BP a sudden rise of Lake Constance, a sign of cooling, forced people to abandon the Arbon-Bleiche 3 lakeshore village.

title: Ötzi the Iceman dies in the Alps

facts.text: Ötzi, the oldest known human mummy, was killed on the Tisenjoch pass, on today's Austrian–Italian border, about 5,300 years ago.
He carried both a copper axe and a flint knife.
Glacier ice at about 3,210 m preserved him as a natural mummy; einkorn and barley grains found beside him reflect Neolithic farming.

title: Mount Rainier collapse and Osceola Mudflow

facts.text: About 5,000 years ago a huge part of Mount Rainier slid away, taking about 490 m off its summit.
The debris avalanche fed the Osceola Mudflow, which reached the sites of today's Tacoma and south Seattle.

title: Proposed Burckle crater impact

facts.text: The Holocene Impact Working Group proposes that a 29 km undersea feature in the southwest Indian Ocean is an impact crater about 5,000 years old.
Its backers link it to floods that affected Sumerian civilization.

title: Campo del Cielo iron meteorite fall

facts.text: A shower of iron meteorites fell on the plains bordering Argentina's Chaco Province, the field called Campo del Cielo.
A fragmented meteorite blasted over a dozen craters in central Australia; the field is no older than about 4,700 years.
It is one of the few impacts in a populated area and among the best-preserved small crater fields.

facts.text: Cerro Blanco in Argentina produced the largest known eruption of the Central Andes, a VEI 7 event that formed its youngest caldera and thick ignimbrites.
It released about 110 km³ of tephra, comparable to the largest Holocene eruptions.
Its tephra is a regional time marker, and subsidence still under way beneath the volcano may be a lasting effect.
